text: Every piece of quantum computing literature uses the same compact notation for vectors and their conjugate partners. Learning to read and manipulate it fluently is as foundational as learning array notation was for ordinary programming.

A ket, written ket-psi, is just a column vector — ket-zero is 1,0, and ket-one is 0,1, written vertically. A general qubit state is a, b, also vertical. A bra, written bra-psi, is the conjugate transpose of that same ket: lay it on its side as a row, and take the complex conjugate of each entry, flipping the sign of any imaginary part. That conjugation is exactly what's needed to make lengths and probabilities come out as real, non-negative numbers instead of possibly-complex ones.

Putting a bra next to a ket forms the inner product — multiply corresponding entries and sum. Check the four basic inner products of ket-zero and ket-one: bra-zero ket-zero is 1, bra-one ket-one is 1, and the cross terms, bra-zero ket-one and bra-one ket-zero, are both 0. Each basis vector has inner product 1 with itself and 0 with the other — together, that's what 'orthonormal basis' means.

Now a less trivial case. Recall ket-plus equals ket-zero plus ket-one, over root 2 — as a vector, about 0.7071 and 0.7071. Computing bra-zero ket-plus gives 1 times 0.7071 plus 0 times 0.7071, which is 0.7071. Squaring that magnitude gives 0.5 — exactly the probability of measuring ket-plus as outcome 0 in the computational basis, matching what you'd get directly from the amplitudes.

Dirac notation isn't decoration — it's the notation every quantum SDK's underlying math maps onto directly: state vectors, unitary matrix multiplication, and inner products for computing measurement probabilities. Reading a circuit diagram or a paper fluently means instantly recognizing that an inner product is an overlap between two states, whose square is a probability.
Next lesson looks at the computational basis itself — why it's the default for readout, and why it's a choice rather than the only valid way to describe a qubit.
